clauses.text: When an AI listens to a Texas doctor's visit and drafts the note,
who checks it before it goes in the record?
A September post from the medical school at UTHealth Houston says UT Physicians is working toward adopting Epic's ambient listening platform as a unified system,
after pilots of DAX and Abridge.
Its plans call for physicians across the practice to eventually get it,
along with an Epic refresher.
On October 8th, 2026,
a company called Abridge announced an agreement with the University of Texas System's health AI initiative.
Abridge says the agreement is a framework that lets UT health institutions access Abridge,
and each one keeps its own decision.
Abridge says its tool maps the AI's draft back to source data,
so a clinician can verify it.
Texas law, in effect since September 1st, 2025,
lets a practitioner use AI for diagnosis under conditions that include reviewing all records created with AI.
That law is written around diagnosis,
and the bill text doesn't say whether a visit note counts.
No source here says how often drafts are checked,
or how accurate they are.
The vendor's design and the statute's review condition both point the check at the clinician.
None of these sources says how well that check works.

story_contract.opening_question: When an AI listens to a Texas doctor's visit and drafts the note, who checks it before it goes in the record?

story_contract.action: UT Physicians is working toward Epic's ambient listening platform, Abridge announced an agreement with the UT System initiative and S.B. 1188 conditions AI diagnostic use on review of AI records.
story_contract.change: Visit notes at UT health institutions can be drafted by AI from the conversation for a clinician to verify.
story_contract.affected_people: Physicians who review the drafts and the patients whose visits are the source. No person is named or drawn.
story_contract.consequence: A clinician is expected to review a draft note that software wrote from the visit.
story_contract.source_limit: The Abridge claims are the vendor's own. The school page gives no date, accuracy or time figure. The bill is written around diagnosis and doesn't say whether a visit note counts.
story_contract.closing_answer: The vendor's design and the statute's review condition both point the check at the clinician, and none of these sources says how well that check works.

captions.text: When an AI listens to a Texas doctor's visit and drafts the note,
who checks it before it goes in the record?
A September post from the medical school at UTHealth Houston says UT Physicians is working toward adopting Epic's ambient listening platform as a unified system,
after pilots of DAX and Abridge.
Its plans call for physicians across the practice to eventually get it,
along with an Epic refresher.
On October 8th, 2026,
a company called Abridge announced an agreement with the University of Texas System's health AI initiative.
Abridge says the agreement is a framework that lets UT health institutions access Abridge,
and each one keeps its own decision.
Abridge says its tool maps the AI's draft back to source data,
so a clinician can verify it.
Texas law, in effect since September 1st, 2025,
lets a practitioner use AI for diagnosis under conditions that include reviewing all records created with AI.
That law is written around diagnosis,
and the bill text doesn't say whether a visit note counts.
No source here says how often drafts are checked,
or how accurate they are.
The vendor's design and the statute's review condition both point the check at the clinician.
None of these sources says how well that check works.
